question: Why do the September 2026 numbers look so low?

sql:
WITH source AS (
    SELECT c.*, p.channel, p.metro,
           coalesce(pay.paid, 0) AS paid_to_date,
           coalesce(pay.paid, 0) + c.reserve_amount AS incurred,
           c.close_date - c.report_date AS days_to_close
    FROM claims c
    JOIN policies p USING (policy_id)
    LEFT JOIN (
        SELECT claim_id, sum(amount) AS paid FROM claim_payments GROUP BY claim_id
    ) pay USING (claim_id)
)
SELECT CAST(date_trunc('month', loss_date) AS DATE) AS period, count(*) AS value
FROM source
WHERE loss_date >= DATE '2026-01-01'
  AND loss_date <= DATE '2026-09-30'
GROUP BY ALL
ORDER BY ALL

WITH numerator AS (
    WITH source AS (
        SELECT c.*, p.channel, p.metro,
               coalesce(pay.paid, 0) AS paid_to_date,
               coalesce(pay.paid, 0) + c.reserve_amount AS incurred,
               c.close_date - c.report_date AS days_to_close
        FROM claims c
        JOIN policies p USING (policy_id)
        LEFT JOIN (
            SELECT claim_id, sum(amount) AS paid FROM claim_payments GROUP BY claim_id
        ) pay USING (claim_id)
    )
    SELECT CAST(date_trunc('month', loss_date) AS DATE) AS period, count(*) AS value
    FROM source
    WHERE loss_date >= DATE '2026-01-01'
      AND loss_date <= DATE '2026-09-30'
    GROUP BY ALL
    ORDER BY ALL
),
denominator AS (
    WITH source AS (
        SELECT * FROM exposure_monthly
    )
    SELECT CAST(date_trunc('month', month) AS DATE) AS period, sum(policies_in_force) AS value
    FROM source
    WHERE month >= DATE '2026-01-01'
      AND month <= DATE '2026-09-30'
    GROUP BY ALL
    ORDER BY ALL
)
SELECT period, 1000 * numerator.value / nullif(denominator.value, 0) AS value
FROM numerator JOIN denominator USING (period)
ORDER BY ALL

report.interpretation: Why September 2026 looks low. I counted claims by loss date, with claim count and claim frequency (claims per 1,000 policy-months) as the agreed metrics. I compared September with Jan–Aug 2026. The extract date is 2026-09-30.
report.answer: September is partly an artifact of incomplete data, and partly a comparison against an unusually high July–August. September has 308 claims, a frequency of 4.33 per 1,000 policies. The Jan–Jun range was 313–407 claims and about 5.6–6.9 per 1,000. The data-quality check estimates only about 79% of September's claims have been reported yet, because claims are reported a median of 4 days after the loss. Scaling up, September would be about 390 claims, which is in the normal range. Later-reported causes are hit hardest. Bodily injury is 7 against a Mar–Jun monthly average of about 19, and fire, hail and liability are also well below average. Claims for losses in the last week of September are mostly still to come. July (606) and August (444) were elevated, probably by a weather or catastrophe surge. I didn't test that, so the drop from August looks steeper than it is. Expect September to rise as late claims arrive. Don't read it as a real improvement.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Late reporting makes the latest month incomplete
hypotheses.evidence: About 79% of September claims are estimated reported. Bodily injury, fire and hail counts are well below normal. Gross-up gives about 390 claims.
The claims table has no duplicate rows.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Comparison base inflated by a July–August surge
hypotheses.evidence: July had 606 claims and August 444, against 313–407 in Jan–Jun. I did not identify the cause of the surge.

hypotheses.hypothesis: A real drop in claim activity
hypotheses.evidence: The adjusted level is only slightly below the Jan–Jun average (about 5.5 against about 6.2 per 1,000 by rough estimate). That gap can't be separated from noise until the month is complete.

data_quality_issues.issue: September 2026 is incomplete because claims are reported late. Roughly 21% of its claims are not yet reported.
data_quality_issues.impact: Claim counts, frequency and incurred for September are understated. Loss ratio is affected too.
